lesson.title: Naming Nothing: The Power of Anonymous Functions
lesson.summary: Lambda functions let you write small, throwaway functions inline as expressions, without the ceremony of a full def statement.
lesson.body:
Every function you have written so far with def has a name, a body of statements, and lives on as long as its enclosing scope does. Sometimes, though, you need a function for exactly one purpose, used in exactly one place, and giving it a permanent name feels like overkill. Python's lambda keyword lets you write that kind of function as a single expression, right where you need it. A lambda is still a function object, just like one created with def. It takes arguments, it returns a value, and it can be called, assigned, or passed around like any other value, which is why lambdas only make sense once you already understand functions and expressions.

The syntax is deliberately minimal: lambda arguments: expression. There is no return keyword, because the value of the expression is automatically returned. There are no parentheses around the parameter list, and critically, the body must be a single expression, not a sequence of statements. Consider:

square = lambda x: x * x
print(square(5))

Trace: square is bound to a function object. Calling square(5) evaluates 5 * 5, which is 25, so this prints 25.

Lambdas earn their keep as short lived arguments to other functions, rather than as named, reusable pieces of logic. A common example is customizing how a list gets sorted:

words = ["banana", "kiwi", "apple", "fig"]
words.sort(key=lambda w: len(w))
print(words)

Trace: the key function is applied to every element to decide sort order. "banana" has length 6, "kiwi" has length 4, "apple" has length 5, "fig" has length 3. Sorting those lengths ascending gives fig, kiwi, apple, banana, so the printed list is ['fig', 'kiwi', 'apple', 'banana']. The lambda saved us from defining and naming a get_length function elsewhere in the file just to use it once. The logic lives exactly where it is used, which keeps related code close together and avoids cluttering the namespace with one use helper names.

A lambda can take more than one argument, separated by commas, just like a regular function's parameter list. The body is still exactly one expression:

add = lambda a, b: a + b
print(add(3, 4))

Trace: calling add(3, 4) evaluates a + b with a bound to 3 and b bound to 4, giving 7, so this prints 7. Here the lambda was assigned to a name, add, which works, but it is worth knowing that assigning a lambda to a variable this way is exactly equivalent to writing def add(a, b): return a + b, and most Python style guides recommend the def form whenever the function is going to have a lasting name, saving lambda specifically for the case where the function is created and used immediately, inline, as an argument to something else.

Lambdas do have real limits, and knowing them will save you frustration. Because the body is a single expression, you cannot put an assignment, a loop, or several statements chained together inside one. If the logic needs more than one line of real work, write an ordinary function with def instead. There is no performance or capability advantage to forcing complex logic into a lambda, only a readability cost. In the next chapter, you will see why this matters so much: lambdas are most useful specifically because Python treats functions as values that can be handed to other functions, which is the foundation of higher order functions.
